newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong graft buster vows no letup after handover.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong graft buster vows no letup after handover.

text.p: Hong Kong's chief graft buster, undeterred by China's imminent takeover of Hong Kong, said on Tuesday there would be no let-up in the war against corruption after the historic handover.

With less than a month to go before Britain hands its 156-year-old colony back to China, Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) chief Lily Yam sought to allay fears that the change might weaken the ICAC as a weapon against graft.
"The ICAC remains steadfast. We have every determination to pursue corruption -- whatever his (the suspect's) background, whatever his connections," Yam told reporters.
Many in Hong Kong have voiced fears that the change of sovereignty will open the door to pernicious influences from the communist-ruled mainland, such as its rampant corruption.
Surveys by the ICAC and by the Baptist University of Hong Kong have shown corruption is uppermost on people's minds when they think of the handover.
But Yam said it would be business as usual for the ICAC.
The commission has cleaned up government and the police, and helped keep down corruption in the private sector since being formed in 1974.
It has far-reaching powers and has successfully smashed corruption cases involving government lawyers, top civil servants, diplomats and organised triad crime gangs.
However, Yam said the ICAC relied on the backing of the new Special Administrative Region (SAR) government that will rule Hong Kong from July 1.
"We need the continued determination of the SAR government and the staunch support of the public," Yam said.

The government-in-waiting has already been formed under the leadership of Tung Chee-hwa, a former shipping tycoon who was chosen last December by a China-controlled committee to run Hong Kong after the British leave.
